lesson.grammar_point: indirect questions: could you tell me what / where / if + subject + verb

listenings.text: Thank you very much for this interesting talk. I work in a pain clinic in Ankara, and we see many patients with nerve damage after diabetes, not leprosy, but I think the mechanism is similar. My question is about your sample. You said you had sixty patients, but how many of them were women? Because in our clinic, women report much more pain than men, and we are not sure if this is biology, or if men simply do not talk about it. So, do you think gender could be a factor in your results, or did you not look at that?

Hello, yes, two quick questions from me. First, a practical one: where can we find your protocol? Is it published, or is it only on the poster? And second, maybe a more difficult one. You measured pain with a scale from zero to ten. But many of our patients cannot read, and they do not understand numbers very well. So how do you know that the patients understood the scale? Did you use pictures, faces, anything like that? Thank you.

paras: Most people think listening is about understanding every word. In a fast Q&A, that is impossible, even for native speakers. Good listeners do something different: they listen for the key words. The first one is the question word at the start or the end: what, how, why, do you. The second one is the topic, usually a noun: the sample, the dose, the scale. With these two, you already know most of the question.

The second strategy is to predict. Before your talk, write down the five questions that people will probably ask. Most questions in a Q&A are about the sample, the method, the limits and the next step. When you know the context, your brain can infer the words you missed. Pace and accent are less of a problem when you know what is coming.

The third strategy is to ask early. If you cannot keep up with a long question, do not wait until the end and hope. Say "Sorry, could you tell me what you mean by...?" or "So you'd like to know if... Is that right?" Nobody in the room will think you are weak. They will think you want to answer the real question, and that is what a good scientist does.

choices: You need to understand every word of a question before you can give a good answer to it in a Q&A.
Key words, prediction and early repair help you understand fast questions.
Asking a speaker to repeat a question is a sign of weakness.
